analysis.one_liner: Requires offshore oil drilling to use the best available blowout preventers and emergency shutoff equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: it sat in committee from June 2010 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Filed months after the 2010 Gulf of Mexico oil spill, the bill would have ordered the Interior Department to write rules requiring every offshore drilling and production operation to have safety management systems, blowout preventers, and backup emergency shutoff equipment such as acoustic shutoff technology, using the best available and safest technology. The rules would apply to all new operations immediately and to existing ones six months after issuance, with a required technology review every five years. The bill never left the House Natural Resources and Energy and Commerce Committees, where it was referred on the day it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishermen, tourism businesses, and offshore rig workers, who bear the damage when a blowout dumps oil into the ocean; also taxpayers and coastal residents who absorb cleanup costs and regional economic losses from spills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fishermen, and offshore workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires all offshore oil and gas drilling and production operations to have safety and environmental management systems in place, including blowout preventers and backup emergency shutoff equipment such as acoustic shutoff technology.

Mandates that safety equipment use the best available and safest technologies, with the Interior Secretary required to issue the regulations within six months of enactment and apply them to all new operations and to existing operations after a six-month grace period.

Requires a review of blowout preventer and emergency shutoff technology every five years, so requirements keep pace with improvements rather than freezing at one-time standards, and directs the Energy Department to independently identify the best available technology for Interior to use.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators would pay to install and maintain backup emergency shutoff equipment and to comply with new safety management rules, costs that could be passed into energy production expenses; drilling operations during the rulemaking period would face added regulatory requirements.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to all existing operations within six months of the rule, which would impose retrofit and compliance costs on offshore drillers that could be passed into production costs.

The bill requires acoustic shutoff technology among the backup equipment but leaves it to regulators to weigh different requirements for different environments and depths, so the value and feasibility of specific equipment in very deep water would be determined by rulemaking rather than the statute.
The bill is a technology mandate only; it does not address spill liability caps, inspection funding, or other spill-response issues raised by the 2010 disaster.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is lower risk of a catastrophic blowout that damages coastlines, fisheries, and local economies, balanced against real compliance costs for offshore operators. The design is narrow and technology-focused, with a clear deadline and periodic reviews, which limits the cost side. Its main weakness is what it leaves out: liability and broader safety oversight are untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, one sent it to a subcommittee in early July, and neither committee ever reported it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 29, 2010 and referred the same day to the House Natural Resources Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
On July 2, 2010 the Natural Resources Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and the action history shows no markup, committee vote, or floor action after that.
The Congress ended January 3, 2011 with the bill still in committee, so no vote was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided new backup shutoff equipment requirements and a six-month regulatory deadline. Coastal communities got no additional statutory protection.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 29, 2010 and took no further action on the bill.

against.name: House leadership

against.what_they_did: Never moved the bill to the floor; the House took up broader spill-response legislation instead, and this bill remained in committee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan (4 of 253 House Democrats and 2 of 178 House Republicans), and since the bill never reached a vote, the chambers' party split was never tested.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas drillers and operators
industries.note: The bill would have required them to install backup emergency shutoff equipment and safety management systems across all offshore operations within about six months. Their interest in avoiding those compliance costs ran against the public's interest in preventing blowouts and spills.
Stricter blowout prevention and shutoff requirements would have reduced the risk of spills that shut down fisheries and coastal tourism, as the 2010 Gulf spill did.
A requirement for best-available blowout preventers and acoustic shutoff technology would have created demand for advanced safety equipment.
